text: Mykola Shevchenko (Ukrainian) / Age: 22
Rank/Position: Red Army soldier, submachine gunner (PPSh)
Civilian Occupation: Shoemaker's apprentice
Origin: Around Poltava, Ukrainian SSR
Mykola shouldn't be here. Not in the karmic, spiritual sense, like <i>“no child of God deserves
to be dragged into a slaughterhouse”.
Not even because, as a Ukrainian, he never truly felt part of this conflict with
the Third Reich and its allies.
No, he shouldn't be here for a much simpler reason.
With a father of his rank, conscription was supposed to be the kind of thing that happened
to ordinary people.
Not to him.
And yet he was here.
And the worst part was this: he had
volunteered. Mykola had a best friend. Bohdan. Neither of them had siblings, so when they
met — four or five years old — they filled that empty space in each other's lives. They became
brothers by choice. Mykola's parents warned him. Be careful who you attach yourself to.
A boy with Bohdan's background can bring trouble.
The source of that suspicion was obvious.
Mykola's father had been transferred from Kyiv as the regional economic officer for the Party committee.
The entire weight of strategic production — military equipment — rested on his shoulders.
Bohdan's father, on the other hand, was nothing more than a factory locksmith.
“What does it say about us,” his mother would ask, “that you keep company with some no-name
scum?”
Mykola didn't care.
He spent every hour he could with Bohdan.
Often at Bohdan's home.
Their conditions were modest compared to Mykola's, but the atmosphere was better.
Much better.
There was singing.
Card games that stretched late into the night,
dinners that felt like feasts. And Mykola was always welcome at their table.
He would never admit it to his mother, but to Mykola, home-cooked food meant
Aunt Daryna's cooking, not the lukewarm slop that was placed in front of him at home.
As the years went on, the bond between the two boys became the subject of
endless gossip. Classmates. Even teachers. People talked. Which is why it was almost funny that in
the end it was a girl who came between them.
Oksana. She and her family — mother, father, four younger siblings — had moved into the
city from a small farm near Poltava after the state stripped them of almost
everything they owned. Their lives crossed
because of chess. More precisely, because of the Poltava chess club. Mykola wasn't much of a player.
Bohdan was. Some people called him a once-in-a-generation talent. A boy who was always at
least four moves ahead. At least until Oksana walked into the club. After a lazy game against
two much younger children,
Mykola got bored. He poured himself tea and laced it with vodka. Then he went looking for
Bohdan in the Friday-night swirl of the House of Culture. When he found him, Bohdan was
wearing an expression Mykola had never seen on his face before — certainly not during chess.
Concentration mixed with worry. Across from him sat a strawberry-blonde,
freckled girl. And from the number of pieces still standing on the board, it was clear
she was giving Bohdan a serious challenge. Mykola sipped his spiked tea and stared at her
without shame. Oksana lost, in the end. Bohdan won.
But she entered their lives anyway. Irreversibly,
and the same was true in the other direction.
From the start, Mykola felt like a third wheel whenever the three of them were together.
Bohdan and Oksana had more in common than just chess.
There was a harmony between them that made even the boys' legendary friendship feel…
smaller.
But when Mykola was alone with her —
rare moments, usually because Bohdan was stuck working overtime at the factory —
Mykola began to believe that Oksana wasn't indifferent to him. Not to his temper, not to his loudness,
not to his reckless jokes and his crude humor. Not to the way he filled a room.
In the end, it turned out he hadn't just imagined it.
Two weeks after Bohdan asked for Oksana's hand — and she said yes —
she invited Mykola for a walk.
At the bank of the Vorskla, Mykola slept with the fiancée of his childhood best friend.
He didn't fool himself into thinking it meant anything to her beyond one last indulgence.
But the way she turned away afterward, as if
nothing had happened, still hurt. The next time he heard from her was three
months later, when conscription was already sweeping through Poltava. On paper,
Mykola had nothing to fear. His father was a respected figure. Some people would
say a useful idiot, inside the Soviet war machine.
All Mykola had to do was avoid attention. Stay away from crowds. Keep off the streets.
So when the knock came at the front door one morning, panic filled the house. Then relief.
No officers on the threshold.
It was Oksana.
She sat in the salon and didn't waste time.
In her usual blunt, unsoftened way, she told Mykola she was pregnant, and that the child
was almost certainly his, not Bohdan's.
Mykola, stunned,
asked what she expected him to do with that information.
Oksana answered calmly.
<i>“Do what's right.
Go in Bohdan's place.”
Mykola called her insane.
He said it was the craziest thing he had ever heard. That's when she played her ace.
Either Mykola takes Bohdan's place, or Oksana tells him everything.
And then Mykola will spend the rest of his life living with what he did.
“Imagine Bohdan out there,” she said. “Bleeding out while laying in the mud,
thinking that the best friend he loved like a brother and the woman he adored betrayed him.”
So Mykola said yes and took Bohdan's place.
Now, shivering in bone-freezing cold, gripping his weapon until his fingers ache, he understands
how stupid it was to agree.
But it's easy to be noble and generous when you're warm. When your stomach is full. When
you aren't living under the simple fact that any second now someone can put a bullet through you.
“Bohdan — come here!” one of his comrades calls.
Mykola needs a full second to realize the words are meant for him.
He turns toward the voice. A cigarette is offered. He takes it with gratitude.
Thin blue smoke rises gracefully into the steel-gray sky.
